lesson.scenario: A router scores a tenant key against four storage nodes and preserves ownership when an unrelated node leaves.

steps.title: Candidates listed
steps.narration: The router evaluates the same eligible node set for tenant T9.
steps.outcome: No ring traversal or shared token placement is needed.
steps.invariant: Every router must use the same hash, weights, and membership epoch.

steps.title: Scores computed
steps.narration: The key-node hash yields deterministic weighted scores.
steps.invariant: The highest score wins; identical inputs must produce identical rankings.

steps.title: Replicas ranked
steps.narration: A is selected as the second owner for redundancy.
steps.outcome: The top two deterministic scores define the replica set.
steps.invariant: Selecting multiple owners uses score order without a separate placement structure.

steps.title: Unrelated node leaves
steps.narration: C leaves, but C was not an owner for T9.
steps.outcome: T9 remains on B and A with no movement.
steps.invariant: A membership change affects only keys for which the changed node alters the top ranks.

steps.title: Primary leaves
steps.narration: When B leaves, A becomes primary and D becomes the second owner.
steps.outcome: Only keys owned by B need reassignment.
steps.invariant: Naive rendezvous routing evaluates every candidate, so large fleets need hierarchical or indexed variants.

production.scenario: A mobile chat service uses rendezvous hashing to keep websocket sessions sticky to the same hub while still moving only a few reconnecting users when autoscaling adds capacity.
